Adult California headlightfish (Diaphus theta) attain a maximum standard length of ten centimeters [Li = ten centimeters], a size that places them among the smaller mesopelagic lanternfishes that undergo pronounced diel vertical migration. This ultimate length, derived from a total length measurement of 11.4 centimeters based on photographic evidence, reflects a moderately elongate body form typical of the genus. Females of this species achieve an ultimate wet weight of ten grams [Wwi = ten grams], a value estimated from length–weight relationships that incorporate a condition factor specific to this myctophid. Adult body mass in D. theta is thus modest compared to some of its larger congeners, which may exceed thirty grams in asymptotic weight. The observed size structure of spawning aggregations in the California Current suggests that individuals attaining these maximum dimensions are relatively rare in the population, with most breeding fish falling somewhat below the upper size limit.

Puberty in males and females of Diaphus theta is reached at a standard length of 6.5 centimeters [Lp = 6.5 centimeters], marking the transition to reproductive competence. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 2.7 grams [Wwp = approximately 2.7 grams], a figure that aligns well with the allometric scaling relationship used to estimate mass from length in this species. The attainment of sexual maturity at this moderate body size likely reflects the selective pressures of a high-mortality pelagic environment, where early reproduction can offset the risks associated with postponed breeding. Field collections indicate that individuals at this pubertal size are the smallest actively spawning fish in the population, with fully mature gonads observed in specimens as small as 6.5 centimeters standard length. The length-based maturity schedule of D. theta appears to be relatively invariant across its range, suggesting a genetically canalized developmental program.

The maximum reproductive output of California headlightfish was evaluated under controlled conditions at a stable water temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, females were estimated to produce approximately 1,300 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 1,300 eggs per clutch], with a reproductive frequency of three clutches each year [F_R_i = three clutches each year]. This reproductive strategy, which yields roughly one clutch every four months, is characteristic of an iteroparous mesopelagic species that spawns multiple times throughout the year. The daily reproduction rate implied by these values is relatively high for a myctophid of this body size, reflecting the species' adaptation to a productive upwelling ecosystem. The 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C] temperature used in these estimates corresponds closely to the mean annual temperature of the species' preferred daytime depth stratum in the California Current system.

Neonatal wet weight at birth in Diaphus theta is estimated at 0.00052 grams [Wwb = 0.00052 grams], a remarkably small value derived from the species' egg diameter of approximately one millimeter. This tiny birth mass reflects the production of pelagic, yolk-sac larvae that undergo a lecithotrophic stage before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The larval period culminates in metamorphosis, which occurs at 71 days from birth  when reared at a water temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]. This relatively extended larval duration, spanning over two months under these thermal conditions, is consistent with the slow developmental rates typical of cold-water myctophids. The metamorphic transformation at this age marks a critical ecological transition from a pelagic larval habit to a more juvenile morphology capable of undertaking diel vertical migrations.

Maximum lifespan in Diaphus theta was recorded at 730 days [am = 730 days] under natural thermal conditions of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]. This two-year longevity places the species among the shorter-lived members of the family Myctophidae, many of which can survive for three to five years in cooler waters. The life history strategy characterized by a modest maximum size, early puberty at 6.5 centimeters standard length, and relatively short lifespan of 730 days [am = 730 days] suggests a high intrinsic rate of population turnover at a temperature of 7.9 °C [T = 7.9 °C]. This demographic pattern is well suited to the variable productivity regimes of the California Current, where rapid population responses to favorable conditions can be advantageous.
